Sparse deconvolution with a fixed PSF via L0-penalised GLMs

Source: R/L0glm_sparse_deco.R
L0glm_sparse_deco.Rd

Estimates the latent, un-blurred single or multichannel spike train \(a\) from an observed signal \(y\) that is assumed to follow the convolution model $$y \;=\; X(g)\,a + \varepsilon,$$ where \(X(g)\) is a Toeplitz design matrix that contains time-shifted copies of a known point-spread function \(g\) (PSF, a.k.a. convolution kernel) and errors \(\varepsilon\) are assumed to be drawn from an exponential family error distribution (e.g. Poisson, Gaussian, Gamma, Inverse Gaussian). The coefficient vector (or matrix) \(a\) is found with best-subset or best-subset of group selection via L0glm.

Usage

L0glm_sparse_deco(
  y,
  family = poisson(identity),
  kernel = NULL,
  kernelfunc = function(x) convkernel("gaussian", L = length(x), params = list(sigma =
    6), perc = 0),
  L = if (!is.null(kernel)) length(kernel) else 51,
  X = NULL,
  baseline = NULL,
  nknots = max(4L, floor(nrow(as.matrix(y))/500)),
  IC = "gic",
  grouped = TRUE,
  control.solver = do.call("control.solver.gen", list(solver = "eigen", method = 1L))
)

Arguments

y

Numeric vector or matrix; the observed (blurred) signal. A matrix is treated as \(n \times m\) outcome channels.

family

A GLM family object with an identity link specifying the desired error distribution (e.g. `poisson(identity)`, `gaussian(identity)` or `Gamma(identity)`).

kernel

Either a numeric vector that is the fixed PSF in forward time order, or `NULL` together with `L` and `kernelfunc`, in which case the PSF is generated on the fly (useful for simulations).

kernelfunc

A function that returns a length-\(L\) numeric vector when called as `kernelfunc(1:L)`. Defaults to a Gaussian with sigma=6.

L

Desired kernel length when `kernel` is `NULL`.

X

Optional. A sparse design matrix that overrides the automatic call to convmatrix. This is useful when you need time-varying PSFs.

baseline

Character. One of NULL (no baseline, default), "intercept" (a single constant column), or "bspline" (cubic B-spline basis). The baseline columns are prepended to the Toeplitz design and are always included in the model. Their fitted contribution is used as an offset in the L0glm_deco_estkernel kernel-update step.

nknots

Integer >= 4. Number of spline knots to use when baseline = "bspline". With nknots < 4 and baseline="bspline" baseline is changed to intercept.

IC

Information criterion for the penalty preset; see information_criteria.

grouped

Logical, passed unchanged to L0glm.fit, specifying whether to perform grouped L0 feature selection, i.e. best subset of group selection (BSGS), in case there are multiple outcome channels. Defaults to TRUE.

control.solver

Optional solver-control list passed to L0glm.fit. By default this uses Eigen sparse Cholesky LLT with AMD ordering. For strictly banded PSF designs, users can pass control.solver.gen("eigen", method=1L, NaturalOrdering=TRUE) to request Eigen natural ordering.

Value

A list with

coef_spikes

Estimated un-blurred spikes, i.e. the coefficients for design matrix X_spikes (same shape as y).

coef_baseline

Estimated baseline coefficients for baseline design matrix X_baseline.

fitted_values

\(X a\), the fitted signal.

fitted_baseline

\(X a\), the fitted baseline

deviance

Residual deviance of the fit.

X_spikes

Toeplitz design matrix for the spikes.

X_baseline

Design matrix for the baseline.

Details

The algorithm is inspired by the L0-penalised deconvolution approach of de Rooi & Eilers (2011) for chromatographic pulse trains, but it leverages the general machinery of L0glm. This results in the following improvements:

  • No manual tuning of the regularisation parameter is required; instead it can be preset to approximate information criteria such as GIC, AIC, BIC, EBIC or MBIC

  • Both single channel data with L0 best subset selection or multichannel data with grouped L0 best subset of group selection are allowed for

  • Any exponential-family noise model with an identity link can be used (Poisson, Gaussian, Gamma, ...)

  • The underlying sparse design is handled by Eigen's efficient sparse Cholesky solver, enabling large problems to be tackled quickly

In the non-negative-matrix-factorisation (NMF) literature this model would be referred to as single-atom convolutional NMF or sparse convolutional dictionary learning, whereby a one-dimensional signal (or multichannel matrix) \(y\) is approximated as \(W(g)\,H\), where \(W(g)\) is a banded Toeplitz matrix that holds time-shifted copies of a fixed dictionary atom/PSF \(g\), and \(H\) is a (potentially multi-column) matrix of sparse, non-negative activations \(a\). However, relative to standard single-atom convolutional NMF we offer several extensions:

  • Optimal sparsity: we do not fix the sparsity level of the activations \(a\) in advance; instead we let L0glm perform best-subset or best subset of group selection through an L\(_{0}\) or grouped L\(_{0}\) penalty,

  • General noise models: any exponential-family likelihood with an identity link is supported (Poisson, Gaussian, Gamma, inverse-Gaussian, ...), instead of only Gaussian (Euclidean-distance NMF) or Poisson (NMF with KL divergence)

  • Speed: the Toeplitz design is solved by sparse-Cholesky linear algebra rather than multiplicative updates, giving orders-of-magnitude speed-ups on long signals

Methodologically this could be referred to as generalised / deviance matrix factorisation (Kidzinski et al. 2022; Castiglione et al. 2024; Wang & Carvalho 2023), specialised to the case where \(W\) is a Toeplitz single-atom convolutional dictionary matrix and where the matrix factorisation is solved with an L\(_{0}\) or grouped L\(_{0}\)-penalised generalised linear model (GLM) fit via adaptive ridge regularised iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS).

A classical baseline for Poisson deconvolution is the Richardson-Lucy algorithm (Richardson 1972; Lucy 1974). In modern terms, Richardson-Lucy equals Kullback-Leibler NMF with multiplicative updates (Lee & Seung 1999) and factor matrix \(W\) constrained to be a convolution matrix. Empirically, L0glm_sparse_deco() has much better support recovery, attains much lower reconstruction error and is dramatically faster thanks to (i) closed-form sparse linear solves, (ii) the automatic selection of the penalty parameter through information-criterion presets, and (iii) the possibility to exploit grouped-sparsity when several channels are deconvolved jointly.

See also

L0glm_deco_estkernel for the complementary "estimate-the-kernel" step, L0glm_blind_deco for the full alternating blind deconvolution, convmatrix (design matrix) and convkernel (PSF generator).

Examples

## ------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 1  Simulate a blurred spike-train with a BIGAUSSIAN PSF & Poisson noise
## ------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(Matrix)
library(splines)
set.seed(123)
family <- poisson(identity)

## --- true point-spread function (PSF) -----------------------------
L       <- 51                       # kernel length
sigma1  <- 1.25                     # left-hand sigma
sigma2  <- 5                        # right-hand sigma
g_true  <- convkernel("bigaussian", L,
                      params = list(sigma1 = sigma1,
                                    sigma2 = sigma2),
                      perc   = 0)   # already centred

## --- latent sparse spike-train ------------------------------------
n        <- 10000                   # timepoints
npeaks   <- round(n / 10)           # 1000, ~10 % non-zero
idx      <- sample(n, npeaks)
amps     <- sample(1000:100000, npeaks)
a_true   <- numeric(n);  a_true[idx] <- amps   # true spikes

## --- baseline -----------------------------------------------------
baseline <- "intercept" # or "bspline" or NULL 
if (!is.null(baseline)) {if (baseline=="intercept") {
  X_baseline <- Matrix::Matrix(1, n, 1, sparse = TRUE)
  a_baseline <- 5000
} else if (baseline=="bspline") {
  nknots <- max(4L, floor(n/500))
  X_baseline <- splines::bs(seq_len(n), df = nknots, degree = 3)
X_baseline <- Matrix::Matrix(X_baseline, sparse = TRUE)
  a_baseline <- runif(nknots, min = 2000, max = 6000)
}} else { X_baseline <- NULL }

## --- generate blurred, noisy observations -------------------------
X_sim  <- convmatrix(g_true, n)
if (!is.null(X_baseline)) { X_full <- cbind(X_baseline, X_sim)
a_full <- c(a_baseline, a_true)
y_baseline <- as.vector(X_baseline %*% a_baseline) # noiseless baseline  
} else { 
  X_full <- X_sim
  a_full <- a_true
  y_baseline <- rep(0, n) }

y_true <- as.vector(X_full %*% a_full)    # noiseless convolution
y      <- rpois(n, y_true)                # with Poisson noise


# quick sanity plot
plot(y, type = "l", ylim = c(0,max(y)), main = "Simulated blurred spike train with baseline in red")
lines(y_baseline, col="red")

## ------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 2  Deconvolution with the known PSF
## ------------------------------------------------------------------------

fit <- L0glm_sparse_deco(y, kernel = g_true,
                         family = poisson(identity),
                         baseline = baseline, 
                         IC = "gic")
a_est_baseline <- as.vector(fit$coef_baseline) 
a_est <- as.vector(fit$coef_spikes)
sum(a_est!=0) 
# 992 with NULL baseline, 1030 with intercept baseline, 1043 with bspline baseline

## ---------- summary statistics ------------------------------------
n_true <- sum(a_true != 0)
n_est  <- sum(a_est  != 0)
tp     <- sum(a_true != 0 & a_est != 0)
precision <- tp / n_est
recall    <- tp / n_true
F1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
R2p <- 100 *
  summary(lm(a_true ~ 0 + a_est))$r.squared
R2p
# 99.80369 with NULL baseline, 96.70126 with intercept baseline, 97.15414 with bspline baseline

## ---------- scatter-plot with true vs. estimated peak areas -------
main_expr <- bquote(
  atop("Poisson L0-glm deconvolution with known PSF",
       atop("true vs. estimated peak areas",
            italic(R)^2 == .(sprintf("%.2f", R2p)) * "%" ~ "|" ~
              "peaks:" ~ .(n_true) ~ "(true)," ~ .(n_est) ~ "(est.)" ~ "|" ~
              "F1 =" ~ .(sprintf("%.2f", 100 * F1)) * "%")))

plot(a_est, a_true,
     xlim = range(a_est, a_true),
     ylim = range(a_est, a_true),
     pch  = 16, col = "blue",
     xlab = "estimated value",
     ylab = "true value",
     main = main_expr)
